summary:
The week of September 14-21, 2026 showed data center resistance consolidating at every level of government, with Washington itself now joining in: the U.S. House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act 417-3 on September 16 — a rare near-unanimous vote directing states to consider standards ensuring data centers cover their own grid-upgrade costs — while California Governor Gavin Newsom, facing a September 30 deadline on a package of data center oversight bills including SB 1168, SB 886, SB 887 and AB 2383, declared that regulating data centers is 'now a bipartisan issue.' That bipartisan turn was echoed in New Hampshire, where Senate President Sharon Carson announced on September 18 that the Republican-majority Senate will pursue AI data center moratorium legislation for the 2027 session, aligning the legislature with Governor Ayotte's planned budget moratorium after a Democratic moratorium bill failed earlier in the year.
The local wave continued at an unrelenting pace, with new moratoriums or bans enacted in at least ten jurisdictions in a single week: Woodford County, Kentucky became the first Kentucky county to permanently ban data center construction; Manatee County, Florida, Statesville, North Carolina, Clarendon County, South Carolina, Lima and McDonald Village in Ohio, Foley, Alabama, Woodburn, Oregon, and Marysville, Kansas all adopted temporary pauses; and North Little Rock, Arkansas confined data centers to heavy industrial zones. The movement is also reaching the country's densest tech markets: San Francisco supervisors introduced an interim moratorium on new data centers and expansions on September 15, Portland's city council unanimously declared its intent to pursue hyperscale restrictions and refused developer NDAs, and Philadelphia's mayor stood up a data center impact task force. In Virginia's data center heartland, Prince William County's planning commission recommended ending by-right development ahead of a September 22 board hearing, with Loudoun County preparing similar amendments. Notably, the wave is not uniform: Massena, New York rejected a proposed moratorium to clear a roughly 400 MW project, and Santa Cruz County, California declined to require voter approval for AI data centers — signs that communities weighing concrete economic benefits sometimes choose development.
On the state-policy front, enforcement and process moves mattered as much as new bills. Texas Governor Greg Abbott ordered the Texas Water Development Board on September 14 to penalize data centers that ignored mandatory water-use surveys — only about 28 percent responded over three years — threatening permit ineligibility and referral to prosecutors, a notable escalation from a state still courting the industry. New Jersey saw its first explicitly AI-focused freeze proposal, A5482, which would pause approvals and incentives for AI data centers over 10 MW for six months. In New Mexico, the state supreme court lifted the stays that had frozen permitting for the 2.45 GW Project Jupiter Stargate campus, letting construction-well drilling and the air-permit process resume even as the statewide moratorium bill heads toward the 2027 session — and Google simultaneously announced it is exploring a Lea County data center, underscoring that development pressure and restriction are rising together.
Trends to watch: Newsom's September 30 sign-or-veto decisions on the California data center package; New York Governor Hochul's continuing deliberation over the Responsible Data Center Development Act with her Executive Order 62 permit moratorium still in force; the Prince William County board vote on September 22 and Loudoun's October 6 debate, which together could end by-right data center development in the industry's largest market; final moratorium votes queued in Leon County, Florida (October 13), Moffat County, Colorado (October 13), Beaufort County, North Carolina (October 5) and Woodbury, Minnesota (September 23); and whether the House's Ratepayer Protection Act gains Senate traction and turns cost-allocation into the first federal data center standard.
